name: Material variants
summary: Swap the constitutive model (elastic, weakly-compressible fluid, snow plasticity) and study how each behaves and optimizes under the same control task. The most visually striking axis for the demo.

tasks.title: Implement Nondifferentiable Material Variants
tasks.note: Let’s start simple. Implement a nondifferentiable forward simulatiodemonstrating the difference between solids, liquids, and snow. Show these materials under a few different settings. Verify they are behaving as expected. This is primarily a learning task, meant to get a grounding with these new materials, and demonstrate what they look like. Make sure to update the training report, so that I actually learn from this task.

tasks.title: Fluids, snow, and solids as differentiable simulations
tasks.note: These look really cool. Now let’s build a simple differentiable implementation of each and see what it takes to get meaningful gradients. When you tried this before the gradients were bad and the particles exhibited erroneous behavior. Be sure to test iteratively to check that it’s functional, examining images as needed. If we can’t get meaningful gradients just report so honestly and explain or theorize why. Make sure to give some nice visuals and update training materials.

tasks.title: Varying Liquid Viscosity
tasks.note: Implement a simulation of a fluid under varying viscosities and demonstrate the differences in their behavior in a few settings. The viscosity should vary dramatically, like from honey to oil.

tasks.title: Train and Interpolate NNs to Mimic Viscous Liquids
tasks.note: Pick two or three viscosity levels. Run the forward simulations to get example runs. Then instantiate a neural network (of the same size) for each viscosity and replace the implementation of just the particle update step, or a portion of it, with this neural network. Evaluate if the NNs generalize to new starting configurations. Then, finally, see what happens when we interpolate the weights of these neural networks. Will we get liquids that have intermediate viscosity levels? Smoothly?

tasks.title: Train Material Replicating NNs and Interpolate
tasks.note: Good results with the viscous liquids. Now I’d like to see the same thing again but this time train a NN to approximate each of the three materials between fluid, elastic solid, and snow, like we implemented in the “Material Variants” direction’s tasks. After the NNs are able to replicate each of the three material types, once again see if they generalize to new conditions. Then, test the linear interpolating again and see what happens! This is a long and detailed task, so the agent should work carefully to ensure it is implemented well.

rework_history.note: The training on a single drop is too limiting, especially for snow since it hardly even acts like snow in that one drop example. We should show it more examples, and test it on more generalization. And then for the interpolation I think there's a bug, because even in the a=0.00 demonstration the simulation explodes or fails to mimic the GT even though it's shown that the net does actually learn the drop example.

These results are much better -- the a=0.00 and a=1.00 are actually correct now. Only change I'd like to see is that the snow behaves more like snow. Right now it's acting almost like an elastic solid with a little bit more give. Snow shouldn't be able to hold itself in a vertical column while jiggling around, for example. It should crumble.

tasks.title: One NN for Three Materials
tasks.note: Train one neural network to mimic all three materials. The control for which material gets simulated should be a small set of swappable parameters specific to each material. Then attempt the same linear interpolation but just interpolating the swapped parameters. The swappable parameters should be just two of them, no more. Visualize them as a square grid where you show each of those two variables on each axis and the resulting effects. It can be an interactive visualization. Make sure to work hard, this is a tough task. Make sure that at all the edges (parameters set equal to the trained set) the results follow the expected simulation exactly.

tasks.title: Implement Liquids across Viscosity and Surface Tension
tasks.note: Building off the viscosity implementation, add a new parameter to our fluid simulations which introduces surface tension. Then, create some visualizations from different starting conditions of fluids which vary across these two axes -- and create a full 3x3 table showing a fluid for every combination across the two. It doesn't need to be differentiable.

tasks.title: Generalize One NN across Viscosity and Surface Tension
tasks.note: Now I want you to train a neural network to replicate the physics of these fluids. Specifically, following the same protocol as in the “One NN for Three Materials Task”, I want you to have one shared network that learns to replicate three different conditions: high viscosity low surface tension (ST), low viscosity high ST, and low viscosity and low ST. The only difference should be two parameters that we vary with the network, and all other parameters are shared, so that those two parameters reflect our viscosity and surface tension results. Also, use lower maximum surface tension than you do here, or interpolate more smoothly at low values, because even the second ST frames here are very high and effectly act like the max ST ones. Regardless, use the NN with smooth interpolation the two parameters to build a large 5x5 grid showing how it performs at every combination compared to GT, and let’s see if it can also generalize to the held out corner of high viscosity high ST.

tasks.title: Train One NN to Mimic Viscosity and ST
tasks.note: Train one neural network to mimic liquids with different viscosities and surface tensions across the axes of low ST high viscosity, high ST low viscosity, and low ST low viscosity, but hold out the low ST low viscosity corner. Keep 2 free parameters which designate these conditions which also gets passed to the model. The NN should learn the entire material physics, replacing the equation entirely, but should still exist within the entire MPM scaffolding. Then, demonstrate whether the NN can interpolate between conditions and generalize to the held-out corner in a big 5x5 grid of results.

tasks.title: Interactive Simulation of One Material
tasks.note: The purpose of this task is to start shifting attention on the demo. To start, let's  make an interactive simulation, small scale, for a single material (maybe elastic solid, like stiff rubber). It's not obvious to me whether making it interactive will be easier using the standard equations, or using a NN that learns the grid update. But in the end we would like to be able to ship actual interactive simulations running in real time on the web, including ones with small learned nets. The purpose of this task is to get just a single small interactive demo showing a conversion of the Taichi setup to something suitable for this format, which should be the centerpoint of the final task page for this. It needs to be efficient, and smooth, real-time, but it can be still just a simple 2D grid. The task should be clear about how this was achieved.

tasks.title: WebGPU port of the interactive simulation
tasks.note:
Port the interactive elastic simulation to a WebGPU compute path and repeat the same analysis the JS port did, so the three routes are directly comparable on the same machine.

WHY: the JS port is exact but capped at ~1150 particles at 60fps, because dt=1e-4 forces 167 substeps/frame. The canonical Taichi/CUDA path is WORSE (~345us/substep, flat from 500 to 16384 particles) because it pays a ~56us kernel launch per kernel per substep from Python -- the 4090 is idle. WebGPU avoids exactly that by recording many dispatches into ONE command buffer submitted once per frame.

CONFIRMED AVAILABLE (measured 2026-08-16, do not re-litigate): navigator.gpu works in the dashboard's Electron pane on the same RTX 4090 -- adapter nvidia/lovelace, requestDevice OK, atomic<u32> shader compiles, and timestamp-query is available for real GPU-side profiling. The earlier task's claim that WebGPU was unavailable was wrong.

THE CRUX: WGSL has NO atomic float add ('atomic' only supports i32, u32 or vec2u), and P2G scatters mass and momentum as floats. Start with FIXED-POINT integer atomics -- mass into u32, momentum into i32 because it is signed -- with a large multiplier. Spend a BOUNDED amount of time finding a scale that works well enough to demonstrate the route is viable; this task is not the optimisation study. Note that a CAS-loop float add (bitcast + atomicCompareExchangeWeak) also compiles and is exact in f32 but slower under contention; a quick head-to-head is cheap and would sharpen the planned follow-up.

VERIFY the same way the JS port did: traj_rmse against canonical sim.physics on a matched initial condition, read against the simulator's own self-noise band, shown as motion side by side. Fixed-point quantisation CHANGES the numerics, so this verification is the point, not a formality. Report a particle/fps budget and where the frame time goes (use timestamp-query, not wall clock).

A dedicated deep analysis of the atomic-add implementation is a planned follow-up task. This one only has to prove the route works and say what it costs.

tasks.title: Sand as a fourth canonical material, and four materials in one grid
tasks.note:
Add SAND as a fourth canonical material, and show all four materials in one grid for the first time.

1) SAND IS A PROMOTION EVENT, not a task-local material. sim/physics/ freezes exactly fluid, elastic and snow. Adding sand goes through sim/physics/PROMOTION.md: it is ground truth, the golden signatures pass, the version bumps -- and sand needs its OWN signature (it should pile at an angle of repose and hold it, not spread like a fluid). Drucker-Prager style granular plasticity is the usual choice; justify whatever is picked.

2) REPORT SAND'S STABLE dt AS A FIRST-CLASS RESULT. This is not a footnote -- it may set the frame budget for the entire Demo MVP. A shared grid means ONE timestep, so the stiffest material present dictates the cost for everything in the scene. Snow already forces 333 substeps/frame (vs 167 elastic, 139 fluid), and NOT because of its E: hardening h = exp(xi*(1-Jp)) with xi=10 makes compacted snow roughly 3x stiffer than elastic, so snow runs at 0.08 of the linear CFL limit where the others sit at 0.21-0.26. If sand hardens similarly, its dt could be as small or smaller. Measure it and say so plainly.

3) MULTI-MATERIAL IN ONE GRID. Canonical simulate() runs one material at a time. Add a per-particle material id and a step that branches on it so a single grid can hold all four at once. Interactions between materials may be weird or unphysical -- that is explicitly fine. The goal is to show multiple materials coexisting in one grid for the first time.

4) VISUALS of all four with simple particle rendering, colours for distinction: elastic red, sand yellow, water blue, snow white. Reuse the renderer from the interactive port as a starting point if it helps. Rendering polish is deliberately held out for a later task -- dots and colour are enough.

DO NOT change fluid / elastic / snow parameters. Add sand alongside them so the WebGPU port's generated params are unaffected by the version bump.

tasks.title: The Demo MVP: four materials on WebGPU, live on the Demo page
tasks.note: Develop a first instantiation of the demo, by combining all four materials (sand, water, elastic solid, snow) in one interactive grid running in real time using WebGPU. The user should be able to add them to the grid and watch them interact / watch the simulation unfold. And at a minimum a reset button. The user should also be able to drag and interact with the scene.

tasks.title: Propose new rendering for each of the four materials
tasks.note:
Do not update the actual demo page yet. Even though this task is meant to lead to updates there, the objective for now is to just propose improved rendering for each of the four materials. Only after we finalize a nice appearance for each, which may take a sequence of tasks, will we incorporate it into the demo page. This is the start of that sequence. The main issue is that all the materials currently look the exact same, only differing in color. Some thoughts of where to start:
1. Elastic solids can have a strong border to separate it, and the interior should be less mushy looking.
2. The current material appearance is best fit for snow -- mushy and diffuse textured. The others should change and be more individually customized.
3. Water should be more smooth and clear. For this material we actually did a whole deeper rendering work on it, so you may be able to take inspiration from there. More clear and fluid-like. Right now it looks like a smoothie.
4. Sand should be granular, like sand is. Maybe render it as particles or macroparticles with random changes in the size of each granule and irregularities. It should be fine-grained.

tasks.title: Improve material realism in behavior
tasks.note:
This task is meant to influence the demo, but should not yet be incorporated into it. We are going to try and improve the standard physics for each of the materials to make them more realistic. Currently, snow and sand are quite accurate. The issue with water is that it's a bit too mushy and sticky. It should be more smooth flowing. Also, rubber is currently kind of weird. It can compress so that the starting mass ends up taking far less area, which is weird. It also breaks too easily. 
Finally, it'd also be cool to see density. Sand and rubber should sink in water, but snow can float. 
For this task you may change the canonical definitions of the materials. That's the point of the task.
